submission.natural_language_explanation: The negative pole is a two-token phrase detector: it fires on a token that completes a specific memorised pair begun by the immediately preceding token, either an attached in-word completion ('target'->'_link', 'neuro'->'feedback', 'nanot'->'ubes', 'vac'->'u'/'ole') or the second word of one of the model's memorised collocations ('North'->'American'/'Atlantic', 'mental'->'health', 'ground'->'state', 'real'/'mean'->'time', 'far'/'right'->'away', 'capable'->'of', 'realized'->'that'). The trigger list is idiosyncratic rather than semantic or frequency-driven ('South American', 'North Dakota', 'New York', 'ground truth', 'mental illness', 'dark matter' and generic frequent bigrams like 'of the' stay at baseline), so the pole is retrospective: it confirms that the token just read completed a learned unit, and on a 73k-token broad scan its top activations sit a median +0.91 above those same tokens' context-free baselines.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The nanoscale transport laboratory at the coastal research institute has spent nearly a decade studying how heat moves through extremely thin films. Their work began with a straightforward observation: when a metal film is only a few dozen atoms thick, its thermal conductivity falls well below what classical models predict. In the spring of 2019 the group installed a dilution refrigerator in the basement, rebuilt the vacuum chamber, and began measuring samples at temperatures approaching a few thousandths of a kelvin.

The experiments were slow and often failed. Moisture contaminated the chamber, the wiring picked up vibration from the building's ventilation system, and the calibration drifted overnight whenever the pumps cycled. Postdoctoral researchers took turns sleeping beside the apparatus so that someone could record each reading by hand. After two years of false starts the team settled on a procedure that reliably produced clean data: anneal the sample, cool it slowly over six hours, and repeat every measurement three times.

The most striking result came from samples in which carbon nanotubes had been grown directly onto the substrate. Because the tubes carry heat efficiently along their length but hardly at all across it, the film behaved less like a uniform sheet than like a bundle of parallel wires. The group published a short paper describing the effect and then spent a further eighteen months trying to explain it.

Below roughly four kelvin, the measurements showed that the electrons in the film settle into a well defined ground state, and the thermal signal falls almost to nothing. The drop is sharp, reproducible, and it agrees with the group's numerical model to within the stated experimental error. Above that temperature the signal returns gradually, as though the material were remembering, one scattering event at a time, how it used to conduct.

Not everyone was convinced. A rival laboratory argued that the effect could be explained by oxidation at the film edges, and the two groups exchanged several polite but pointed letters. The dispute was eventually resolved by a third team, which repeated the measurement with a completely different contact geometry and obtained the same curve.

The institute has since expanded the project. New samples are grown by chemical vapour deposition rather than by hand, and a small machine learning model now flags readings that look suspicious before they reach a human. The older researchers remain sceptical of the software, but they admit that it catches errors faster than they do. Work on the next generation of films is already under way, and the group expects to publish again within the year. A follow-up grant will fund two more refrigerators and a dedicated technician, which should roughly double the throughput of the older apparatus.
